name: Proving it looks right
intro: For engineers: how the software factory checks built screens against a reference screenshot (measured, judged, accepted), how the checker itself is proven with planted defects, and one real request run end to end.
facts: Real bugs found by running it

scenes.name: Sanjeev Gulati
scenes.line: Building software factories on Claude Code
scenes.say: Sanjeev Gulati · AI Coding Expert
scenes.voice: In my last video, I showed you a software factory, built on Claude Code. This time, I want to tackle its weakest link.

scenes.say: What you asked for, and what the AI called done
scenes.voice: Be honest. How many times have you handed an AI a Figma file, or a screenshot... and it said, done? And then you actually looked at it. The names are wrapping. The table's way too tall. Nothing quite lines up. And this isn't made up. It's a real attempt, from my own factory.

scenes.title: Proving it, not trusting it
points: Verifying the verifier with planted defects.
A request that failed twice before it passed.
The same idea for APIs, data and reports.
scenes.voice: So how do you prove a screen looks right, without a person checking every pixel? In this video, I'll show you the design, how I proved the checker itself works, a real request that failed twice before it passed... and how the same idea works for APIs, too.

scenes.title:
Proving it looks
right
scenes.say: Checking built screens against a reference screenshot, and proving the checker works.
scenes.voice: In a software factory, verification is everything. And for user interfaces, it's been the weakest link. So... let's fix that, and then prove it actually works.

scenes.title: Scripts can't see
scenes.define: The factory could prove the text, the test ids and the tests. It couldn't prove a screen looks like the design. So a person looked, and where verification stops, autonomy stops.
scenes.voice: Here's the honest starting point. The factory could already prove a screen had the right text and the right test ids, and that the tests passed. But it couldn't tell you whether the screen actually looked right. So, a person had to look. And wherever verification stops... autonomy stops too.

scenes.title: Three layers
points: A script: position, size, words, colour, similarity. Same input, same answer.
A separate checker agent, by eye, against a checklist. Every finding cites evidence.
A person sees reference, built and difference side by side, then approves.
scenes.voice: So the idea is three layers. First, measured. A script checks what can be measured, and gives the same answer every time. Second, judged. A separate agent looks at the images, and has to cite evidence for every finding. And third, accepted. A person sees the reference, the result, and the difference, side by side.

scenes.title: From screenshot to baseline
scenes.key: You: approve the contract, then the resultScripts measure; agents build and judge
scenes.say: Screenshot in, baselines out
scenes.voice: Here's how it fits into the pipeline. A screenshot attached to the issue becomes the reference. The visual spec turns it into a contract, and a person approves that, before anything is built. The plan gives the page a visual gate. The checker measures, and judges. After the tests, the verifier runs again. And when the person approves the result, those screens become baselines.

scenes.say: Present, geometry, text, colour, similarity: every number in a report
scenes.voice: The measured layer is one small script. It renders the screen in headless Chrome, then for each region in the contract, it checks five things. Is it there. Is it in the right place. Does it say the right words. Is it the right colour. And does it look similar. Every number goes into a report.

scenes.title: Plant the defects
scenes.say: A verifier nobody has tested is an opinion.
scenes.voice: Now, here's the part most teams skip. A verifier nobody has tested... is just an opinion. So I tested it the way you'd test any other code.

scenes.say: Planted: an element moved 24px. Caught: geometry and similarity
scenes.voice: I took a screen the factory had already built, and planted one defect at a time. Like this one. The totals moved twenty-four pixels. The region goes red on both sides, and the difference panel shows exactly what moved.

scenes.say: Planted: the accent colour swapped. Caught: colour
scenes.voice: A swapped accent colour. Caught by the colour check. The difference is measured, not eyeballed.

scenes.say: Planted: a row wraps. Caught: similarity
scenes.voice: A table row that wraps onto two lines. The box barely moved... but similarity caught it.

scenes.say: Six of six defects caught, zero of three false alarms
scenes.voice: Six planted defects, and all six were caught. And just as important, three harmless changes, like different sample data or a sub-pixel shift... and zero false alarms. It runs in presubmit, so if anyone weakens the verifier, the build fails.

scenes.title: Before it gates anything
scenes.say: 6 of 6 caught, 0 false alarms, identical reports
scenes.voice: And it's deterministic. The same build, verified twice, gives a byte-for-byte identical report.

scenes.title: Build this, matching the screenshot
scenes.say: A request with a reference screenshot attached.
scenes.voice: Okay. Now, let's run a real request through it... end to end.

scenes.say: A screenshot attached to the issue: the reference
scenes.voice: The client attaches a screenshot to the issue, and then writes what they want, in plain words.

scenes.say: Reference saved; contract written
scenes.voice: The intake saves that screenshot with the spec, and the visual spec agent writes a contract from it.

scenes.say: The first contract: the heading's ink, not the heading; a sample-data total
scenes.voice: And here's something I didn't plan for. The first contract the agent wrote was wrong. It measured the heading's text instead of the heading itself, and it demanded a total that only existed in the sample data. Approve that, and a correct build would have failed three times.

scenes.say: Fixed in the skill, not in the result: the meta loop
scenes.voice: So I didn't patch the contract. I fixed the skill that writes contracts. That's the meta loop, working. And the second contract got it right.

scenes.say: Approved before any code exists
scenes.voice: The client approves the contract, along with the requirements, before a single line of code exists.

scenes.say: The plan's visual gate: Cat 4
scenes.voice: The plan gives the page section a fourth gate. A visual check, against the reference.

scenes.say: The inner loop: failed, failed, passed
scenes.voice: And this is where it gets interesting. The checker failed the page twice, for two completely different reasons.

scenes.say: First failure, measured: the table 465px tall against 320px
scenes.voice: The first time, the measured layer caught it. Names were wrapping, and the table was four hundred and sixty five pixels tall, against three hundred and twenty in the reference.

highlight: The verifier passes, but only barely
scenes.say: Second failure, judged: the verifier passed, the checker's eye didn't
scenes.voice: The second time... the verifier actually passed. The maker had overcorrected. Tiny text, cramped rows. The numbers squeaked through, but the checker's judgement didn't. That's exactly why there are two layers.

scenes.say: Attempt 2: every box green, and still not right
scenes.voice: Look at them side by side. Every box is green... but the table has shrunk, and the text is tiny. A script on its own would have shipped this.

scenes.say: Outer loop: evidence, tests, visual-verify, preview
scenes.voice: On the third try, it passed. Then the outer loop ran everything again. The evidence, the tests, and the verifier, on its own.

scenes.say: Reference, built, difference: every region passes
scenes.voice: Reference, built, and difference. Every region green. The only differences left are font rendering, because the runner draws text with Linux fonts.

scenes.say: The gate notice shows reference vs built
scenes.voice: And that image goes straight into the gate notice. The person approving doesn't have to dig for anything.

scenes.say: The built screen, running
scenes.voice: Here's the dashboard, running.

scenes.say: Approved screens become baselines, in the merge request
scenes.voice: And when it's approved, those screens become baselines. The merge request carries them, so the next change to this screen gets checked against them, strictly.

scenes.kicker: What running it for real taught me
scenes.title: Three lessons
points: A git quirk dropped the reference. 'This stage may not write that file' is what exposed it.
The agent's first contract was wrong. Fixed in the skill, and caught at the gate.
macOS and Linux draw text differently: designs are measured, baselines compared.
scenes.voice: Running it for real taught me three things. A git quirk silently dropped the reference. The factory's own guardrail is what exposed it. An agent's contract can be wrong, and that's exactly why a person approves it. And a screenshot from one machine never matches pixels from another.

scenes.title: The same pattern, everywhere
points: Reference: a screenshot. Measured: regions. Kept: approved screens as baselines.
Reference: the spec. Measured: status, schema, contract. Kept: recorded responses.
Reference: an agreed sample. Measured: counts and totals. Judged: the rest.
scenes.say: Agree a reference, measure what you can, judge what you can't, keep what a person accepts
scenes.voice: And this isn't only about screens. The pattern is always the same. Agree on a reference. Measure what you can. Judge what you can't. And keep what a person accepts, as the baseline. For an API, the reference is the spec. Status codes, schemas and contracts get measured, a reviewer agent judges the behaviour, and recorded responses become the baselines. And it works the same way for data, and for reports.

scenes.title: What it doesn't do yet
points: Boxes read from an image are approximate: IoU 0.6, not 0.95.
The checker's eye is a model's opinion, forced to cite evidence.
Proven on one dashboard so far. More screens, more evidence.
scenes.voice: Now, the limits. Boxes estimated from an image are approximate, so the tolerance is generous. The judged layer is still a model's opinion, it's just forced to show its evidence. And so far, it's been proven on one kind of screen.

scenes.title: Verification makes it a factory
scenes.say: The code: github.com/sanjeev23oct/software-factory · test drive: login testdrive
scenes.voice: Verification is what turns agents writing code into a factory you can trust. The code is open source, and there's a test drive account if you want to look around. Thanks for watching.
